newsitem.title: FINLAND: Analysts uncertain on Nordic forestry outlook.
newsitem.headline: Analysts uncertain on Nordic forestry outlook.

text.p: Uncertainty still looms over the Nordic forest industry despite a smaller than expected rise in Norscan pulp inventories in October, equities analysts said on Friday.
"We cannot expect an upturn in pulp prices until inventories fall below 1.5 million tonnes and stay there for some time," said Hubert de Marliare, London-based analyst at Paribas.
The price of Nordic softwood pulp is currently about $560 per tonne, down from $1,000 a year ago, analysts said.
Swedish consultancy group Momentum said earlier on Friday North American and Scandinavian (Norscan) pulp stocks rose by 20,000 tonnes in October from 1.73 million tonnes in September.
Marliare said he thought there was a short-term risk that pulp prices could slip further, adding that it tended to be difficult for forestry companies to curtail production in winter months.
"My view is that pulp prices are more likely to go down than up in the short term," he said.
Kleinwort Benson's Denis Christie said earlier this week that pulp prices could fall between $50 and $100 a tonne in the next few months. This is partly because of lower prices in the Far East.
Den Danske Bank's Niels Leth said the Norscan pulp inventories picture changed his view of the pulp price outlook.
"We had seen a high risk that pulp prices would fall during the winter, but now we believe that risk is much smaller," Leth said.
But he warned that the Norscan pulp inventories figures do not tell the whole story, because they only show producers' inventories and not stocks held by pulp users.
"The numbers don't tell how much pulp stocks customers have, and no one knows how much that side accounts for," he said.
Further price pressure could come from additional pulp capacity projected for Asian markets in particular, analysts said.

"There is not much capacity coming on stream in Europe, but if you look at Asia, huge amounts of capacity will come on stream up to 1999," Leth said. "We will see a capacity increase that is higher than consumption growth."
Though Nordic forestry companies have recently weighed in with what some analysts called dismal interim results, share prices have been rising.

Only this week the forestry sub-index in Helsinki has risen approximately six percent, led by the recovery of the share of Europe's biggest forestry firm UPM-Kymmene which has gained 6.7 percent in five days.
Some analysts said the recent positive share price trend in forestries was not justified when viewed against the background of falling pulp and paper prices.
"It would be difficult to see share prices maintaining current levels ... I see them drifting lower," Kleinwort's Christie said.
Analysts also said telecoms group Nokia's surge following its third-quarter results had boosted the Helsinki bourse and particularly UPM-Kymmene, which holds nine percent of Nokia votes.

Finnish analysts were more upbeat on forestry shares. An upturn in domestic paper industry output in September after a one-year fall, and a sharp increase in the industry's raw wood purchases in addition to the latest Norscan data indicated that the sector is gradually recovering, they said.
"I think forestry stocks are a good investment at the moment," said Aktia Bank analyst Paivi Palomaki.
According to Statistics Finland, forest industry output rose 3.1 percent year-on-year in September -- the first month of growth since August 1995.

The forest industry's raw wood purchases from private forests rose to 7.2 million cubic metres in October -- the highest amount in any month during the 1990s, the Finnish Forest Research Institute (METLA) said.
